sources: Brunaux, Jean Louis. The Celtic Gauls: Gods, Rites and Sanctuaries. (London: Seaby, 1988), 68-70.
"Mysticism is a personal engagement with nature that results in a feeling of timeless unity."

"Superstition is a baseless belief or ritualized behavior that often represents a degraded form of an earlier religion. Mythology and ritual are connected, the first being a narrative or narrative sequence, the second being actions or behaviors that evoke or reflect that myth. Certain problems arise in defining and describing Celtic religion. The Celtic peoples did not employ writing, believing that religious secrets were better shared orally. Thus there is little textual evidence for what the Celts believed." (Author's Last Name, Year of Publication)

"What we have was written down after literacy arrived, along with Christianity, in Celtic lands. We also have some texts written by those who were at war with the Celts, including the Roman general (later emperor) Caesar and the army geographer Tacitus."
David Rankine and Sorita d'Este, The Isles of the Many Gods: An A-Z of the Pagan Gods & Goddesses of Ancient Britain and Ireland (London: Avalonia, 2007), 13-14.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Celtic religion has no surviving creation myth. Some scholars think the Celts saw a world that created itself or existed always. The Celts believed in an Otherworld beyond the tangible world. This Otherworld resembled the Aboriginal Dreamtime. It sat contiguous with our world. Deities and other powerful beings dwelt there. They could affect our world only at certain points of time and space. Human beings could enter the Otherworld. Some entered by accident. Others were taken there by a fairy lover or a fairy hostess. The Otherworld looked like this world but more beautiful and changeless. Trees bore blossom and fruit at the same time. No one aged, and death held no domination there. The Celts held no dualistic view of sacred and mundane. The four directions framed a sacred center. That center was a concept rather than a place. It could move, multiply, or leave this world entirely. The great gods lived in the Otherworld. The Celtic peoples shared no single pantheon. Most gods were specific to a region or environment. Celts swore by the gods their people swore by. Some divinities appeared in many places under different names. These included the triple mothers, a horned god, and divinities of rivers. The Celts did not depict their gods in human form. Divinities could shape-shift into human and animal forms. Only after the Roman conquest did Mediterranean-style images appear. The Celts did not bandy about the names of their deities. All words held power, and divine names held far more. Scholars cannot tell if recorded words were divine names or titles. The Celts kept no organized hierarchical pantheon. They saw gods in families, such as the descendants of Danu or Don. The gods lived in mountains, seas, trees, and running streams. This vision, with the divine inside the physical world, is pantheism. The mother goddess made life possible through generosity and fecundity. She was often the ancestor of a whole people or of the gods. Her name appears as Danu, Anu, or Don. Scholars connect her to a central European goddess Dan. Her name survives in rivers such as the Danube and the Don. Most rivers in Celtic lands keep goddess names. Goddesses were often depicted as triple. In Roman times they were the Deae Matres, shown as three women. Male gods offered skill, craft, magic, and poetry. The Celts held rituals in the open air. They gathered at hilltops, wells, and oak groves. Bog bodies show a threefold death of strangling, stabbing, and drowning. Some scholars accept that human sacrifice occurred in times of crisis. Most ceremonies marked the turning of the seasons. Samhain opened winter on November 1. Beltane opened summer on May 1. Imbolc fell on February 1, and Lughnasa on August 1. The festivals tracked season midpoints rather than solstices. The Celts also told tales of Arthur, the Matter of Britain, and the knights of the Round Table. Those tales rest on the power of the goddess of sovereignty. Fairy lore, called the fairy faith by W. Y. Evans-Wentz, formed part of the tradition.

okr.objective: Celtic religion centered on a changeless Otherworld and a decentralized pantheism.
key_results: Celtic religion has no extant creation myth.
The Celtic Otherworld resembles the Aboriginal Dreamtime.
